title: Greetings and names
goal: Greet people, give your name and say where you come from — while discovering Norwegian's biggest gift: its verbs never change according to who is doing the action.
bekal: greet people and say goodbye according to the time of day
give your name with *jeg heter* and where you're from with *jeg kommer fra*
use the six personal pronouns with one and the same verb form

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På studentbyen
dialogs.intro: It's Budi's first day at the Kringsjå student village in Oslo. He is dragging his suitcase up the stairs when someone opens a door.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, jeg er ny. Jeg heter Budi.
lines.id: Yes, I'm new. My name's Budi.
lines.literal: yes, I am new. I am-called Budi.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.id: Nice to meet you! I'm Ingrid.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hyggelig å møte deg. Bor du her også?
lines.id: Nice to meet you. Do you live here too?
lines.literal: pleasant to meet you. live you here also?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Ja, jeg bor i nummer tolv. Hvor kommer du fra?
lines.id: Yes, I live in number twelve. Where are you from?
lines.literal: yes, I live in number twelve. where come you from?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg kommer fra Indonesia. Og du?
lines.literal: I come from Indonesia. and you?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Jeg er norsk. Jeg er fra Bergen.
lines.literal: I am Norwegian. I am from Bergen.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Ja, litt. Men vi snakker norsk, ikke sant?
lines.id: Yes, a little. But we speak Norwegian, right?
lines.literal: yes, little. but we speak Norwegian, not true?

notes: **Jeg heter Budi** literally means "I am called Budi". Norwegian introduces people with the verb *å hete* (to be called) rather than "my name is…". *Navnet mitt er Budi* does exist and is correct, but it sounds stiff — like filling in a form. Use *jeg heter*.

**Here is the big gift.** Look at *jeg er* and *er du* — exactly the same verb form. The same goes for *jeg heter* / *du heter*, *jeg bor* / *bor du*, *jeg kommer* / *kommer du*. Norwegian verbs **do not change at all** according to who is doing the action. No *am/is/are*, no *-s* for he/she/it. One form for all six persons.
**Jeg is pronounced yai**, not "yeg". The *g* in *jeg*, *meg*, *deg* turns into an *i* sound. These are three of the most frequent words in the whole language, so get the sound right now.
**Hvor is pronounced voor.** An *h* in front of *v* is always silent: *hva* → **vah**, *hvem* → **vem**, *hvorfor* → **VOOR-for**. No exceptions.

**Hyggelig** is the most Norwegian word there is. It's used for people, rooms, evenings, conversations — anything that feels warm and cozy. Say it **HÜ-geh-lee**; the final *g* is silent, as in almost every *-lig* ending.

**Jeg er norsk** — languages and nationalities are written with a **small letter** in Norwegian (*norsk*, *engelsk*, *indonesisk*), unlike English. Country names keep their capital: *Norge*, *Indonesia*.

grammars.title: One verb form for everyone
body: This table is why Norwegian feels light in the first week. Read the columns from top to bottom: nothing changes.
after: Compare English (*I am, you are, he is*) or French (*je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes*). Norwegian has scrapped all of that. All you need to learn is **one form per verb**.
The pronoun *de* (they) is pronounced **dee**, and *dere* (you, plural) is pronounced **DAY-reh**. Beginners mix them up because they look alike; they sound quite different.

Norwegian no longer uses the polite *De* for "you". Even with lecturers, doctors or immigration officers, Norwegians say *du*. This isn't rude — quite the opposite: using *De* would sound odd and distant.

grammars.title: Hello and goodbye
body: Norwegian sorts greetings by time of day, but *hei* cuts across all of them and works almost anywhere.

after: Notice that *god* is pronounced **goo** — the final *d* is silent, and the *o* sounds like "oo". Two big Norwegian habits meet in one short word.
*Ha det bra* literally means "have it good" — something like "take care". In fast speech it shrinks to just **hade**, and that's what you'll hear most on the street.

sections.title: Saying where you're from and what you speak

blocks.text: Two patterns are used interchangeably, and they're equally correct:
Notice there's **no article** in front of languages and nationalities: not *jeg snakker det norsk*, just *jeg snakker norsk* — exactly as in English.

sections.title: Why this feels easy for an English speaker

blocks.text: The first unit of most language courses walks you straight into a wall. There's no wall here, and that's no accident — Norwegian and English are close relatives, and three features make the start especially gentle:

items: **Verbs don't change for the person.** English still clings to *I am / he is* and *I eat / she eats*. Norwegian has dropped even that: *jeg spiser, du spiser, hun spiser* — one form, always.
**No separate progressive tense.** *Jeg spiser* means both "I eat" **and** "I am eating", depending on the situation. English makes you choose between *I eat* and *I am eating*; Norwegian doesn't.
**He and she work just as in English** — *han* and *hun* replace a man and a woman, and they change nothing else in the sentence.

blocks.title: What to watch out for
items: Never drop **er** (am/is/are). *Jeg student* is wrong — it has to be *jeg **er** student*. Note, too, that Norwegian drops the article with jobs and roles: *jeg er student*, not "I am a student".
Always name the subject. A casual English "From where?" won't do: Norwegian says *Hvor kommer **du** fra?*
Say every word all the way to the end. The biggest temptation for beginners is to swallow endings, but that's exactly where Norwegian keeps its grammar.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the correct form of *å være*. (Hint: there's only one.)
